content_html:
A 401(k) is a workplace retirement plan that lets you invest part of every paycheck, often with extra money from your employer. This calculator projects how your account could grow between now and retirement by combining four things: what you already have, what you add, what your employer adds and what the investments earn.

How to use this calculator

  1. Current age and retirement age: the number of years in between is how long the account keeps growing.
  2. Annual salary and yearly raise: your contribution is a percentage of pay, so raises increase it automatically.
  3. Current 401(k) balance: include old plans you have rolled in, but not IRAs held elsewhere.
  4. Your contribution: the percentage of pay you defer, counting pre-tax and Roth 401(k) deferrals together.
  5. Employer match and match limit: a common formula is "50% of what you put in, up to 6% of pay". Enter 50 and 6. For a dollar-for-dollar match up to 4%, enter 100 and 4. Use 0 if there is no match.
  6. Expected return and inflation: the return is an assumed long-run average; inflation is used only to show the final balance in today's dollars.
  7. IRS limits: leave this on to cap contributions at the 2026 limits. The limits are held at 2026 levels for every future year, although the IRS normally raises them with inflation.

How the projection works

Each year the calculator works out your contribution as salary × contribution rate, and the employer match as salary × match rate × the smaller of your contribution rate and the match limit. The year's total is split into 12 equal monthly deposits, and the balance grows at the monthly rate equivalent to your annual return, (1 + r)1/12 − 1. Your salary then rises by the raise percentage before the next year starts.

With limits on, three IRS rules apply: your own deferrals cannot exceed the elective deferral limit plus any catch-up amount for your age, your deferrals plus employer money cannot exceed the total annual additions limit (catch-up contributions don't count toward it), and pay above the compensation limit is ignored.

Worked example

A 30-year-old earning $75,000 with $25,000 already saved contributes 10% of pay. The employer matches 50% up to 6% of pay, salary rises 3% a year and the account earns 6% a year until age 67.

  • First year: $7,500 from the employee and $2,250 from the employer.
  • Balance at 67: about $2,102,405, or about $704,270 in today's dollars at 3% inflation.
  • Of that, $496,307 is the employee's own contributions, $148,892 is employer money and $1,432,206 is investment growth.

Cutting the contribution to 6% (still enough for the full match) lowers the balance to about $1,521,943. Dropping to 3% gives up half the match as well and leaves about $868,922.

2026 contribution limits

Limit (2026)Amount
Employee elective deferrals$24,500
Extra catch-up, age 50 or older$8,000
Extra catch-up, ages 60 to 63 (instead of the age-50 amount)$11,250
Total from you and your employer, excluding catch-up$72,000
Maximum compensation counted by the plan$360,000

Starting in 2026, workers whose prior-year FICA wages from the employer exceeded $150,000 must make any catch-up contributions as Roth contributions. That changes how the money is taxed, not how much you can put in, so it doesn't affect this projection.

Tips for using the results

  • Contribute at least enough to get the full employer match. The callout in the results shows how much match you would otherwise miss.
  • Small increases add up. Raising your rate by one percentage point each year until you reach your target is often easier than one big jump.
  • Check the vesting schedule. Employer money may not be fully yours until you have worked a set number of years.
  • Test a range of returns, such as 4%, 6% and 8%, instead of relying on one figure. The results ignore fees and taxes, and actual returns vary from year to year.

faq.question: How much can I contribute to a 401(k) in 2026?
faq.answer: The 2026 employee deferral limit is $24,500. If you are 50 or older by the end of the year you can add a catch-up contribution of $8,000, and if you are 60, 61, 62 or 63 the catch-up is $11,250 instead. Your plan may set lower limits.

faq.question: Does the employer match count toward my $24,500 limit?
faq.answer: No. The deferral limit only covers your own contributions. Employer matching and profit-sharing contributions count toward the separate total limit of $72,000 for 2026, together with your regular deferrals.

faq.question: Should I choose pre-tax or Roth 401(k) contributions?
faq.answer: Pre-tax contributions lower your taxable income now and are taxed when withdrawn. Roth contributions are taxed now, and qualified withdrawals are tax-free. The better choice depends on whether you expect your tax rate in retirement to be higher or lower than today. This calculator treats both the same, because the limit is shared.

faq.question: Why is the balance in today's dollars so much lower?
faq.answer: Prices rise over time, so a dollar decades from now buys less than a dollar today. The calculator divides the future balance by the cumulative inflation over the years until retirement to show roughly what it would buy at today's prices.

faq.question: What happens if I leave my job?
faq.answer: Your own contributions and their earnings are always yours. Employer contributions belong to you once they vest. You can usually leave the money in the old plan, roll it into a new employer's plan or an IRA, or cash it out, which may trigger taxes and an early withdrawal penalty.
